chapter_text:
CHAPTER 2 — यदि जानासि तद् वद (YADI JANASI TAD VADA)

Introduction — पाठस्य परिचयः

The title of this lesson, यदि जानासि तद् वद, means "If you know, then speak." It is at once an invitation and a challenge. In the Indian tradition of learning, a गुरु would often test students with sharp, riddling questions, and the honest refrain of the classroom was exactly this: if you truly know, speak; if you do not know, say plainly 'न जानामि' (I do not know) and ask with humility. This lesson (NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit, Course 309) explores the difference between real knowledge (सत्यं ज्ञानम्) and empty boasting (वृथा गर्वः) through an original simple-Sanskrit dialogue between a proud pandit and a humble farmer, followed by famous public-domain verses on knowledge and disciplined speech, and a grammar section drawing सन्धि, समास, विभक्ति and लकार from the text. The central teaching is twofold: real knowledge shows itself in conduct (आचारे), not in loud claims; and speech must be disciplined — speak when you truly know, and never be ashamed to admit what you do not know.

संवादः — पण्डितः कृषकश्च (An original dialogue: the Pandit and the Farmer)

एकदा कश्चित् पण्डितः ग्रामं प्रति गच्छति स्म। मार्गे सः क्षेत्रे कार्यं कुर्वन्तम् एकं कृषकं दृष्ट्वा सगर्वम् अवदत्।

पण्डितः — भोः कृषक! अहं महान् पण्डितः अस्मि। व्याकरणं जानामि, ज्योतिषं जानामि, तर्कशास्त्रं च जानामि। त्वं किं जानासि?
(O farmer! I am a great pandit. I know grammar, I know astrology, and I know logic. What do YOU know?)

कृषकः — आर्य! अहम् अल्पज्ञः कृषकः अस्मि। क्षेत्रं कर्षामि, बीजं वपामि, धान्यं च प्राप्नोमि। किन्तु भवन्तम् एकं प्रश्नं पृच्छामि। यदि जानासि तद् वद।
(Sir! I am a farmer who knows little. I plough the field, I sow the seed, and I obtain grain. But let me ask you one question. If you know, then speak.)

पण्डितः — पृच्छ पृच्छ! अहं सर्वाणि शास्त्राणि जानामि।
(Ask, ask! I know all the shastras.)

कृषकः — कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्?
(In which month should the sowing of seeds be done?)

पण्डितः — (विचिन्त्य) एतत्... एतत् न जानामि।
(Having thought — This... this I do not know.)

कृषकः — कीदृशः मेघः वृष्टिं ददाति? कीदृशी भूमिः धान्याय योग्या?
(What kind of cloud gives rain? What kind of soil is fit for grain?)

पण्डितः — एतदपि न जानामि।
(This too I do not know.)

कृषकः — आर्य! भवान् बहूनि शास्त्राणि पठितवान्, किन्तु जीवनस्य विद्यां न जानाति। शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते। यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्। एषः एव विदुषः धर्मः। यदि जानासि तद् वद; यदि न जानासि तर्हि मौनं भज।
(Sir! You have read many shastras, but you do not know the knowledge of life. The shastra sits in the book, but knowledge is seen in conduct. Whoever does not know something should say 'I do not know.' This alone is the dharma of the truly learned. If you know, then speak; if you do not know, then keep silence.)

पण्डितः — (सविनयम्) भोः मित्र! अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः। अहं गर्वं त्यजामि। इतः परं यत् जानामि तत् एव वदिष्यामि, यत् न जानामि तत् श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि।
(With humility — O friend! Today you alone are my guru. I abandon my pride. From now on I shall speak only what I know, and what I do not know I shall ask about with reverence.)

शब्दार्थ (Word meanings from the dialogue): सगर्वम् = proudly; अल्पज्ञः = one who knows little; कर्षामि = I plough; वपामि = I sow; वपनम् = sowing; कर्तव्यम् = ought to be done; विचिन्त्य = having thought; मेघः = cloud; वृष्टिः = rain; योग्या = fit, suitable; पठितवान् = has read/studied; आचारः = conduct, behaviour; विदुषः = of the learned (गेन. of विद्वस्); मौनम् = silence; भज = practise, resort to; सविनयम् = with humility; गर्वः = pride; त्यजामि = I abandon; श्रद्धया = with reverence/faith; पृच्छिष्यामि = I shall ask.

Moral of the dialogue (संवादस्य नीतिः): The pandit carried many books in his head but could not answer a single question of living practice; the farmer, who claimed to know little, knew his own work perfectly and — more importantly — knew the discipline of honest speech. True knowledge is proved in conduct and in the courage to say 'न जानामि'. The truly learned person speaks only of what he knows, and learns the rest with humility.

ज्ञान-विषयक-सुभाषितानि (Public-domain verses on knowledge and speech)

1) विद्या विवादाय धनं मदाय शक्तिः परेषां परिपीडनाय ।
   खलस्य साधोर्विपरीतमेतत् ज्ञानाय दानाय च रक्षणाय ॥
   शब्दार्थ: विद्या = learning; विवादाय = for quarrelling; धनम् = wealth; मदाय = for arrogance; शक्तिः = power; परेषाम् = of others; परिपीडनाय = for tormenting; खलस्य = of the wicked; साधोः = of the noble; विपरीतम् = the opposite; एतत् = this (set of three); ज्ञानाय = for (true) knowledge; दानाय = for giving/charity; रक्षणाय = for protection.
   अन्वयः: खलस्य विद्या विवादाय, धनं मदाय, शक्तिः परेषां परिपीडनाय (भवति); साधोः एतत् विपरीतम् — (विद्या) ज्ञानाय, (धनं) दानाय, (शक्तिः) च रक्षणाय (भवति)।
   Translation: For the wicked, learning serves quarrelling, wealth serves arrogance, and power serves the tormenting of others; for the noble it is the very opposite — learning is for wisdom, wealth for charity, and power for protection.
   Moral: The same possessions reveal the character of the possessor. Knowledge used for boasting and quarrelling is the mark of a खल; knowledge used for understanding and service is the mark of a साधु.

2) आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः ।
   बकास्तत्र न बध्यन्ते मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: आत्मनः = their own; मुखदोषेण = by the fault of the mouth (speech); बध्यन्ते = are caught/bound; शुकसारिकाः = parrots and mynas; बकाः = herons; तत्र = there (in that matter); न बध्यन्ते = are not caught; मौनम् = silence; सर्वार्थसाधनम् = the accomplisher of all aims.
   अन्वयः: शुकसारिकाः आत्मनः मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते; बकाः तत्र न बध्यन्ते; (अतः) मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्।
   Translation: Parrots and mynas are caught because of the fault of their own mouths (their chattering); herons, being silent, are not caught there. Silence is the accomplisher of all aims.
   Moral: Careless, showy speech invites trouble; disciplined silence protects. Speak only when speech serves a purpose — and when you truly know.

3) सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात् न ब्रूयात् सत्यमप्रियम् ।
   प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयात् एष धर्मः सनातनः ॥
   शब्दार्थ: सत्यम् = truth; ब्रूयात् = one should speak; प्रियम् = pleasant; न ब्रूयात् = one should not speak; अप्रियम् = unpleasant; अनृतम् = falsehood; एषः = this; धर्मः सनातनः = the eternal law.
   अन्वयः: सत्यं ब्रूयात्, प्रियं ब्रूयात्, सत्यम् अप्रियं न ब्रूयात्, प्रियं च अनृतं न ब्रूयात् — एषः सनातनः धर्मः।
   Translation: Speak the truth, speak what is pleasant; do not speak an unpleasant truth, and do not speak a pleasant falsehood — this is the eternal law.
   Moral: The discipline of speech has two sides — truthfulness and kindness. 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' adds a third: certainty. Speak what is true, kind, and truly known.

4) यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य ।
   एवं हि शास्त्राणि बहून्यधीत्य चार्थेषु मूढाः खरवद्वहन्ति ॥
   शब्दार्थ: यथा = just as; खरः = donkey; चन्दनभारवाही = carrying a load of sandalwood; भारस्य = of the weight; वेत्ता = knower; न तु = but not; चन्दनस्य = of the sandalwood (its fragrance/value); एवम् = in the same way; शास्त्राणि = scriptures/sciences; बहूनि = many; अधीत्य = having studied; अर्थेषु = in their meanings; मूढाः = the deluded; खरवत् = like a donkey; वहन्ति = (merely) carry.
   अन्वयः: यथा चन्दनभारवाही खरः भारस्य वेत्ता (भवति), न तु चन्दनस्य; एवं हि बहूनि शास्त्राणि अधीत्य (अपि) अर्थेषु मूढाः (जनाः) खरवत् वहन्ति।
   Translation: Just as a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows only the weight and not the sandalwood, so those who study many shastras but remain deluded about their meaning merely carry them like a donkey.
   Moral: Reading without understanding is a burden, not knowledge. The pandit of our dialogue carried shastras as the donkey carries sandalwood — the farmer's questions exposed the load.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar drawn from the lesson

(A) सन्धिः (Sandhi). तद् वद itself is a sandhi form: तत् + वद → तद् वद — the voiceless त् becomes voiced द् before the voiced व् (जश्त्व, a व्यञ्जन-सन्धि). Other examples from the lesson: यदि + अपि → यद्यपि (यण्-सन्धि: इ + अ → य्); न + अस्ति → नास्ति (दीर्घ-सन्धि: अ + अ → आ); सर्व + अर्थ → सर्वार्थ (दीर्घ-सन्धि, in सर्वार्थसाधनम्); च + अनृतम् → चानृतम् (दीर्घ); खरः + चन्दन... → खरश्चन्दन... (विसर्ग-सन्धि: ः before च → श्); एतत् + अपि → एतदपि (जश्त्व)। Practise सन्धि-विच्छेद (splitting): identify which joined form came from which words.

(B) समासः (Compounds). शुकसारिकाः = शुकाः च सारिकाः च — द्वन्द्व-समास (both members coordinate); मुखदोषेण = मुखस्य दोषेण — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष; चन्दनभारवाही = चन्दनस्य भारं वहति इति — उपपद-तत्पुरुष; सर्वार्थसाधनम् = सर्वेषाम् अर्थानां साधनम् — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष; अल्पज्ञः = अल्पं जानाति इति — उपपद-तत्पुरुष; तर्कशास्त्रम् = तर्कस्य शास्त्रम् — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष।

(C) विभक्तिः (Cases). चतुर्थी (dative of purpose) dominates verse 1: विवादाय, मदाय, परिपीडनाय, ज्ञानाय, दानाय, रक्षणाय — all mean 'for the sake of ...'. तृतीया (instrumental): मुखदोषेण 'by the fault of the mouth', श्रद्धया 'with reverence'. षष्ठी (genitive): खलस्य, साधोः, आत्मनः, भारस्य, चन्दनस्य. सप्तमी (locative): पुस्तके 'in the book', आचारे 'in conduct', क्षेत्रे 'in the field', अर्थेषु 'in the meanings'. द्वितीया (accusative object): विद्याम्, गर्वम्, बीजम्, क्षेत्रम्।

(D) लकाराः (Verb moods/tenses). लट् लकार (present tense): जानामि (I know — उत्तमपुरुष एकवचन), जानासि (you know — मध्यमपुरुष एकवचन), जानाति (he/she knows — प्रथमपुरुष), कर्षामि, वपामि, तिष्ठति, वहन्ति, बध्यन्ते। लोट् लकार (imperative): वद (speak!), पृच्छ (ask!), भज (practise!)। विधिलिङ् लकार (optative, 'should'): ब्रूयात् (one should speak), वदेत् (one should say)। लृट् लकार (future): वदिष्यामि (I shall speak), पृच्छिष्यामि (I shall ask)। Note how the title compresses grammar and ethics together: जानासि (लट्, do you actually know?) governs वद (लोट्, only then the command to speak).

सारांशः (Summary)

In this chapter you read an original dialogue in which a boastful pandit, who claims mastery of grammar, astrology and logic, is humbled by a farmer's simple practical questions about sowing, clouds and soil. Forced to say 'न जानामि' again and again, the pandit learns the lesson of the title: यदि जानासि तद् वद — speak if you truly know; otherwise admit ignorance and learn with humility. Four classical verses deepen the theme: विद्या विवादाय contrasts the wicked and the noble in their use of learning, wealth and power; आत्मनो मुखदोषेण warns that careless speech traps the speaker as chattering traps the parrot, praising मौनम् as the accomplisher of all aims; सत्यं ब्रूयात् sets the eternal rule of truthful, kind speech; and यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही mocks study without understanding as a donkey's load of sandalwood. The grammar section draws from the lesson itself: जश्त्व and other सन्धि (तत् + वद → तद् वद), समास types (द्वन्द्व, षष्ठी- and उपपद-तत्पुरुष), the dative of purpose and other विभक्ति, and the लकाराः — लट्, लोट्, विधिलिङ् and लृट्. Carry away the twin disciplines of the chapter: prove knowledge in conduct, and govern the tongue by certainty, truth and kindness.

topics.name: यदि जानासि तद् वद — Title and Theme
topics.description: The meaning of the title 'If you know, then speak'; the classroom tradition of testing knowledge through questions; and the chapter's twin themes — real knowledge versus empty boasting, and the discipline of honest speech including the courage to say 'न जानामि'.

topics.name: संवादः — The Pandit and the Farmer
topics.description: The original simple-Sanskrit dialogue in which a boastful pandit, master of grammar, astrology and logic, is humbled by a farmer's practical questions about sowing, clouds and soil, and finally accepts the farmer as his guru and abandons pride.

topics.description: Key vocabulary of the lesson with English meanings — अल्पज्ञः, मेघः, वृष्टिः, आचारः, गर्वः, मौनम्, खलः, साधुः, खरः, अनृतम्, श्रद्धया and other words from the dialogue and the verses.

topics.name: ज्ञान-विषयक-सुभाषितानि — Verses on Knowledge and Speech
topics.description: Four public-domain verses with शब्दार्थ, अन्वय and translation: विद्या विवादाय (the wicked versus the noble), आत्मनो मुखदोषेण (silence protects), सत्यं ब्रूयात् (truthful kind speech), and यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही (study without understanding).

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Sandhi, Samasa, Vibhakti and Lakara
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the lesson: जश्त्व and other सन्धि (तत् + वद → तद् वद, यद्यपि, नास्ति), समास types (द्वन्द्व, षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष, उपपद-तत्पुरुष), the dative of purpose and other विभक्ति, and the लकाराः लट्, लोट्, विधिलिङ् and लृट् with forms from the text.

topics.name: Translation and Comprehension
topics.description: Translating dialogue lines and verses into simple English, doing अन्वय of verses, and answering comprehension questions on the story, the verses, their word meanings and their morals.

chapter_summary.title: यदि जानासि तद् वद (Yadi Janasi Tad Vada) — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit (309) summary for Chapter 2. The chapter teaches, through a witty pandit-farmer dialogue and four classical verses, that real knowledge shows itself in conduct, that boasting is the mark of hollow learning, and that speech must be governed by certainty, truth and kindness — if you know, then speak; if not, say 'न जानामि' and learn with humility.

sections.heading: The title and its challenge
bullets: यदि जानासि तद् वद means 'If you know, then speak' — an invitation to genuine knowledge and a challenge to empty boasting.
In the guru-shishya tradition, knowledge was tested by sharp questions; the honest answer to an unknown question is 'न जानामि'.
The title joins grammar and ethics: जानासि (लट् — do you actually know?) governs वद (लोट् — only then speak).

sections.heading: The pandit humbled by the farmer
bullets: A pandit boasts of knowing व्याकरण, ज्योतिष and तर्कशास्त्र, and mockingly asks a farmer what he knows.
The farmer asks practical questions — the month for sowing, the rain-giving cloud, the soil fit for grain — and the pandit must repeatedly say 'न जानामि'.
The farmer's verdict: shastra sits in the book, knowledge is seen in conduct (शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते).
The pandit accepts the farmer as his guru, abandons pride, and vows to speak only what he knows and to ask about the rest with reverence.

sections.heading: Verses on knowledge and its use
bullets: विद्या विवादाय धनं मदाय...: for the wicked, learning serves quarrel, wealth serves arrogance, power serves oppression; for the noble the same three serve wisdom, charity and protection.
यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही...: one who studies many shastras without grasping their meaning merely carries them, as a donkey carries sandalwood knowing only its weight.
The pandit of the dialogue is the living example of the donkey verse — much text, no understanding, until humility opens real learning.

sections.heading: Verses on the discipline of speech
bullets: आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः: parrots and mynas are trapped by their own chatter; silent herons go free — मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्.
सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात्...: speak the truth pleasantly; never an unpleasant truth nor a pleasant lie — the eternal law of speech.
The chapter adds a third rule of speech to truth and kindness: certainty — speak only of what you truly know.

sections.heading: Grammar from the lesson
bullets: सन्धि: तत् + वद → तद् वद (जश्त्व); यदि + अपि → यद्यपि (यण्); न + अस्ति → नास्ति and सर्व + अर्थ → सर्वार्थ (दीर्घ); खरः + च... → खरश्च (विसर्ग).
समास: शुकसारिकाः (द्वन्द्व); मुखदोषेण, सर्वार्थसाधनम्, तर्कशास्त्रम् (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); चन्दनभारवाही, अल्पज्ञः (उपपद-तत्पुरुष).
विभक्ति: dative of purpose — विवादाय, मदाय, ज्ञानाय, दानाय, रक्षणाय; तृतीया मुखदोषेण; सप्तमी पुस्तके, आचारे.
लकार: लट् जानामि/जानासि/जानाति; लोट् वद/पृच्छ/भज; विधिलिङ् ब्रूयात्/वदेत्; लृट् वदिष्यामि/पृच्छिष्यामि.

key_takeaways: यदि जानासि तद् वद — speak only if you truly know; otherwise say 'न जानामि' and learn with humility.
Real knowledge shows itself in conduct (आचारे), not in loud claims — the boastful pandit failed the farmer's simplest practical questions.
For the noble, learning, wealth and power serve wisdom, charity and protection; for the wicked they serve quarrel, arrogance and oppression (विद्या विवादाय...).
Careless speech traps the speaker as chatter traps the parrot — मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्, silence accomplishes all aims.
Speech has three disciplines: truth, kindness (सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात्) and certainty (speak what you truly know).
Study without understanding is a donkey's load of sandalwood — knowing the weight, not the fragrance (यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही).
Grammar from the lesson: तत् + वद → तद् वद (जश्त्व सन्धि); dative of purpose (ज्ञानाय, दानाय); लकाराः — लट्, लोट्, विधिलिङ्, लृट्.

glossary.definition: 'If you know, then speak' — the title and refrain of the chapter; the rule that speech must rest on real knowledge.
One who knows little (अल्पं जानाति इति, an उपपद-तत्पुरुष compound); how the humble farmer describes himself.
Conduct, behaviour; the place where real knowledge is seen — ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते.
Pride, arrogance; what the pandit abandons at the end of the dialogue (अहं गर्वं त्यजामि).
Silence; praised as सर्वार्थसाधनम्, 'the accomplisher of all aims', in the verse of the parrots and herons.
A wicked person, whose learning serves quarrel, wealth serves arrogance and power serves oppression.
A noble person, whose learning serves wisdom, wealth serves charity and power serves protection.
The fault of the mouth — careless speech; by it parrots and mynas are caught (आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः).
Falsehood, untruth; even a pleasant falsehood must not be spoken (प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयात्).
Donkey; in the verse, the image of one who carries shastras without understanding, knowing only the weight of the sandalwood.
The joining of sounds where words meet; e.g. तत् + वद → तद् वद by जश्त्व, न + अस्ति → नास्ति by दीर्घ-सन्धि.
A compound word; e.g. शुकसारिकाः (द्वन्द्व), मुखदोषेण (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष), चन्दनभारवाही (उपपद-तत्पुरुष).
The dative case, expressing purpose — विवादाय 'for quarrel', ज्ञानाय 'for wisdom', दानाय 'for charity', रक्षणाय 'for protection'.
A tense/mood of the Sanskrit verb: लट् (present — जानासि), लोट् (imperative — वद), विधिलिङ् (should — ब्रूयात्), लृट् (future — वदिष्यामि).
Reverence, trusting faith; the pandit vows to ask about what he does not know श्रद्धया — with reverence.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — यदि जानासि तद् वद (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 2)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give your explanations in English. Refer to the dialogue and the verses in the lesson where needed.

questions.question:
Translate into simple English:
आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः ।
बकास्तत्र न बध्यन्ते मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् ॥
questions.answer: Parrots and mynas (शुकसारिकाः) are caught/bound because of the fault of their own mouths (आत्मनः मुखदोषेण) — their chattering gives them away. Herons (बकाः), which stay silent, are not caught there. Therefore silence (मौनम्) is the accomplisher of all aims (सर्वार्थसाधनम्).
questions.explanation: The verse contrasts chattering birds that get trapped with the silent heron; disciplined silence protects.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of each: गर्वः, मौनम्, मेघः, वृष्टिः, आचारः.
questions.answer: गर्वः = pride/arrogance; मौनम् = silence; मेघः = cloud; वृष्टिः = rain; आचारः = conduct/behaviour.
questions.explanation: All five words occur in the dialogue and verses of the lesson.

questions.question: In one or two sentences, explain the moral of 'मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्' in the context of this chapter.
questions.answer: Careless or showy speech invites trouble, just as chattering gets parrots caught, while the silent heron goes free. The moral is speech discipline: keep silence unless speaking serves a purpose — and speak only when you truly know.
questions.explanation: Links the bird imagery to the chapter's rule 'if you know, then speak; if not, keep silence'.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split) of: (a) तद् वद (b) यद्यपि.
questions.answer: (a) तद् वद = तत् + वद (त् becomes द् before the voiced व् — जश्त्व, व्यञ्जन-सन्धि). (b) यद्यपि = यदि + अपि (इ + अ → य्, यण्-सन्धि).
questions.explanation: Both splits use sandhi rules illustrated in the lesson's grammar section.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and its meaning-role for each word: ज्ञानाय, मुखदोषेण, पुस्तके.
questions.answer: ज्ञानाय = चतुर्थी (dative of purpose) → 'for the sake of knowledge'. मुखदोषेण = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by the fault of the mouth'. पुस्तके = सप्तमी (locative) → 'in the book'.
questions.explanation: चतुर्थी shows purpose, तृतीया shows means/cause, सप्तमी shows place.

questions.question: Explain the verse 'विद्या विवादाय धनं मदाय शक्तिः परेषां परिपीडनाय । खलस्य साधोर्विपरीतमेतत् ज्ञानाय दानाय च रक्षणाय ॥' with its अन्वय. How does it distinguish the खल from the साधु, and how does it apply to the pandit of the dialogue?
questions.answer:
अन्वयः: खलस्य विद्या विवादाय, धनं मदाय, शक्तिः परेषां परिपीडनाय (भवति); साधोः एतत् विपरीतम् — विद्या ज्ञानाय, धनं दानाय, शक्तिः च रक्षणाय। For a wicked person (खल), learning serves quarrelling, wealth serves arrogance, and power serves the tormenting of others. For a noble person (साधु) the same three serve the opposite ends: learning brings wisdom, wealth is used for charity, and power protects others. The verse teaches that possessions are morally neutral — the character of the possessor decides whether they bless or harm.
Applied to the dialogue: the pandit at first used his विद्या for boasting and belittling the farmer — the खल pattern of विद्या विवादाय/मदाय. After being humbled, he vowed to speak only what he knows and to learn with reverence — turning his learning towards ज्ञान, the साधु pattern. The verse thus mirrors the pandit's transformation.
questions.explanation: Requires अन्वय, the खल-साधु contrast, and application to the pandit's change of heart.

questions.question: Write three simple Sanskrit sentences (in Devanagari) about knowledge and humble speech, using vocabulary from the chapter. Give their English meaning.
questions.answer:
1. सत्यं ज्ञानम् आचारे दृश्यते। (True knowledge is seen in conduct.)
2. यः न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्। (Whoever does not know should say 'I do not know.')
3. विद्वान् गर्वं त्यजति, श्रद्धया च पृच्छति। (The learned person abandons pride and asks with reverence.)
Together these state the chapter's teaching: knowledge is proved in conduct, ignorance should be admitted honestly, and learning grows through humility.
questions.explanation: Simple लट्/विधिलिङ् sentences built from chapter vocabulary — आचारः, गर्वः, श्रद्धया, वदेत्.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the verse 'यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य' and state its moral.
questions.answer: Just as a donkey (खरः) carrying a load of sandalwood knows only the weight (भारस्य वेत्ता) and not the sandalwood's fragrance or value (न तु चन्दनस्य), so people who study many shastras without understanding their meaning merely carry them like the donkey. Moral: reading without understanding is a burden, not knowledge; true study grasps meaning and shows in practice.
questions.explanation: The donkey-sandalwood image mocks rote learning; the dialogue's pandit is its living example.

questions.question: In the dialogue, which three practical questions did the farmer ask, and what was the pandit's answer each time?
questions.answer: The farmer asked: (1) In which month should the sowing of seeds be done (कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्)? (2) What kind of cloud gives rain (कीदृशः मेघः वृष्टिं ददाति)? (3) What kind of soil is fit for grain (कीदृशी भूमिः धान्याय योग्या)? Each time the pandit had to answer 'न जानामि' — I do not know.
questions.explanation: The three practical questions expose the gap between bookish learning and the knowledge of life.

questions.question: What does the title 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' mean, and what twofold discipline does the chapter draw from it?
questions.answer: The title means 'If you know, then speak.' The chapter draws a twofold discipline from it: (1) real knowledge must be proved in conduct, not in boasting; (2) speech must be disciplined — speak only of what you truly know, and honestly say 'न जानामि' about what you do not, learning it with humility.
questions.explanation: Definition of the title plus the two central teachings of the lesson.

questions.question: The title 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' means
questions.explanation: यदि = if; जानासि = you know; तद् = then; वद = speak.

questions.question: In the title, the word 'यदि' means
questions.explanation: यदि is the conditional particle 'if'; तद्/तर्हि answers it with 'then'.

questions.question: The main text of this chapter is in the form of a
questions.explanation: The chapter is built around a dialogue between a pandit and a farmer.

questions.question: The central teaching of the chapter is that real knowledge shows itself in
questions.explanation: The farmer says: शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते — knowledge is seen in conduct.

questions.question: In the dialogue, the sentence 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' is spoken by
questions.explanation: The farmer uses the refrain before asking his practical questions.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what should a person honestly say about something he does not know?
questions.explanation: The dharma of the learned is to admit 'I do not know' (न जानामि) and then learn with humility.

questions.question: Which value does the chapter most emphasise in a true seeker of knowledge?
questions.explanation: The pandit's transformation — abandoning गर्व and asking श्रद्धया — shows humility as the key value.

questions.question: In the title, the word 'वद' means
questions.explanation: वद is the लोट् (imperative) form of वद् — 'speak!'.

questions.question: On his way to the village, whom did the pandit meet?
options: a farmer working in his field
questions.answer: a farmer working in his field
questions.explanation: The pandit saw a कृषक working in the field and addressed him proudly.

questions.question: The pandit boasted that he knew
questions.explanation: व्याकरणं जानामि, ज्योतिषं जानामि, तर्कशास्त्रं च जानामि — grammar, astrology, logic.

questions.question: The farmer's first question to the pandit was about
options: the right month for sowing seeds
questions.answer: the right month for sowing seeds
questions.explanation: कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्? — In which month should sowing be done?

questions.question: What did the pandit reply to each of the farmer's practical questions?
questions.explanation: The pandit had to admit 'I do not know' to every practical question.

questions.question: According to the farmer, 'शास्त्रं ____ तिष्ठति' — the shastra sits where?
questions.explanation: शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते.

questions.question: According to the farmer, knowledge (ज्ञानम्) is seen in
questions.explanation: ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते — knowledge is seen in conduct.

questions.question: At the end of the dialogue, the pandit decides to abandon his
questions.explanation: अहं गर्वं त्यजामि — I abandon my pride.

questions.question: In the farmer's self-description, 'क्षेत्रं कर्षामि' means
questions.explanation: कर्षामि (from कृष्) = I plough; the farmer then sows (वपामि) and obtains grain.

questions.question: Whom does the pandit finally call his guru?
questions.explanation: अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः — today you alone are my guru, says the humbled pandit.

questions.question: The pandit vows that in future he will ask about what he does not know
questions.explanation: यत् न जानामि तत् श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि — I shall ask about it with reverence.

questions.question: In the verse 'विद्या विवादाय...', for the noble person (साधु) learning serves
questions.explanation: For the साधु the three serve ज्ञान, दान and रक्षण — the opposite of the खल.

questions.question: According to the same verse, the wealth (धनम्) of a wicked person (खल) serves
questions.explanation: खलस्य धनं मदाय — the wicked person's wealth feeds his arrogance.

questions.question: In 'आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः', the parrots and mynas are caught because of
options: the fault of their own mouths (their chattering)
questions.answer: the fault of their own mouths (their chattering)
questions.explanation: मुखदोषेण = by the fault of the mouth; their own speech betrays them.

questions.question: Why are the herons (बकाः) not caught in that verse?
questions.explanation: The heron's silence protects it — hence मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्.

questions.question: 'मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्' means
options: silence is the accomplisher of all aims
silence is a sign of ignorance
questions.answer: silence is the accomplisher of all aims
questions.explanation: मौनम् = silence; सर्वार्थसाधनम् = the means of accomplishing all purposes.

questions.question: According to 'सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात्...', which of these should one NOT speak?
questions.explanation: न ब्रूयात् सत्यम् अप्रियम् — an unpleasant (harsh) truth should not be spoken; nor a pleasant lie.

questions.question: In the donkey verse, the donkey carrying sandalwood knows only
questions.explanation: भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य — knower of the weight, not of the sandalwood.

questions.question: The verse 'यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही...' compares the donkey to
options: those who study many shastras without understanding their meaning
those who refuse to study at all
those who carry heavy loads for a living
questions.answer: those who study many shastras without understanding their meaning
questions.explanation: अर्थेषु मूढाः खरवद्वहन्ति — deluded about the meanings, they merely carry the texts like a donkey.

questions.question: According to the verse 'विद्या विवादाय...', the power (शक्तिः) of a साधु serves
questions.explanation: For the noble, power exists to protect others, not to oppress them.

questions.question: In 'सत्यं ब्रूयात्...', the phrase 'एष धर्मः सनातनः' refers to
options: the eternal law of truthful and kind speech
the rule of silence in the forest
questions.answer: the eternal law of truthful and kind speech
questions.explanation: The whole discipline of speech — truth spoken pleasantly, no harsh truth, no pleasant lie — is the eternal dharma.

questions.question: The word 'मेघः' means
questions.explanation: कीदृशः मेघः वृष्टिं ददाति — what kind of cloud gives rain?

questions.question: The word 'वृष्टिः' means
questions.explanation: वृष्टिः (from वृष्, to shower) = rain.

questions.question: 'अल्पज्ञः' means
questions.explanation: अल्पम् (little) + ज्ञ (knower): अल्पं जानाति इति अल्पज्ञः.

questions.question: The word 'गर्वः' means
questions.explanation: The pandit says अहं गर्वं त्यजामि — I abandon my pride.

questions.question: The word 'मौनम्' means
questions.explanation: मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् — silence is the accomplisher of all aims.

questions.question: The word 'खलः' means
questions.explanation: खलस्य विद्या विवादाय — the wicked person's learning serves quarrel.

questions.question: The word 'साधुः' in the verse means
questions.explanation: साधोः विपरीतम् एतत् — for the noble person these serve the opposite (good) ends.

questions.question: The word 'खरः' means
questions.explanation: यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही — like a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood.

questions.question: The word 'शुकः' means
questions.explanation: शुकसारिकाः = parrots and mynas, caught by their own chattering.

questions.question: The word 'बकः' means
questions.explanation: बकाः तत्र न बध्यन्ते — the silent herons are not caught.

questions.question: The word 'अनृतम्' means
questions.explanation: प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयात् — one should not speak even a pleasant falsehood.

questions.question: The word 'आचारः' means
questions.explanation: ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते — knowledge is seen in conduct.

questions.question: The word 'कृषकः' means
questions.explanation: कृषक (from कृष्, to plough) = one who ploughs, a farmer.

questions.question: The word 'श्रद्धया' means
questions.explanation: श्रद्धा (reverent faith) in the instrumental case — 'with reverence'.

questions.question: According to the chapter, a person who boasts of learning he does not truly understand is like
questions.explanation: The खर verse: he knows the weight of the texts, not their meaning.

questions.question: A student is asked a question in class and is not sure of the answer. Following this chapter's teaching, the student should
options: admit not knowing and ask to learn
stay quiet and pretend to know
questions.answer: admit not knowing and ask to learn
questions.explanation: यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत् — then learn it with श्रद्धा.

questions.question: The verse about शुकसारिकाः chiefly warns against
questions.explanation: The birds' own mouths trap them — careless speech invites trouble.

questions.question: Why does the chapter treat the farmer as wiser than the pandit?
options: he has practical knowledge of his work and the humility of honest speech
he owns more land than the pandit
he has read more shastras than the pandit
he speaks louder than the pandit
questions.answer: he has practical knowledge of his work and the humility of honest speech
questions.explanation: The farmer knows his own field of work thoroughly and models 'if you know, then speak'.

questions.question: In this chapter, 'speech discipline' (वाक्-संयमः) chiefly means
options: speaking only what one truly knows
questions.answer: speaking only what one truly knows
questions.explanation: The title's rule: if you know, then speak; if not, keep silence or admit ignorance.

questions.question: Which behaviour matches the साधु's use of wealth described in the verse?
questions.explanation: साधोः धनं दानाय — the noble person's wealth is for charity.

questions.question: Which student best shows 'real knowledge' as this chapter defines it?
options: one who answers accurately when asked and admits gaps honestly
one who quotes many books loudly in every discussion
one who never studies but debates confidently
one who memorises texts without knowing their meaning
questions.answer: one who answers accurately when asked and admits gaps honestly
questions.explanation: Knowledge proved in conduct plus honest speech — the chapter's double test.

questions.question: The pandit's opening speech to the farmer shows the खल pattern of the verse because he uses his learning for
questions.explanation: विद्या विवादाय/मदाय — learning used for showing off and putting others down.

questions.question: The सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'तद् वद' is
questions.explanation: तत् + वद → तद् वद: voiceless त् becomes voiced द् before व् (जश्त्व).

questions.question: The change of त् to द् in 'तत् + वद → तद् वद' is an example of
questions.explanation: A voiceless stop becomes its voiced counterpart before a voiced sound — जश्त्व.

questions.explanation: अ + अ → आ (दीर्घ-सन्धि): न + अस्ति = नास्ति.

questions.question: The compound 'शुकसारिकाः' (parrots and mynas) is a
questions.explanation: शुकाः च सारिकाः च — two coordinate members joined: द्वन्द्व.

questions.question: The compound 'चन्दनभारवाही' (carrying a load of sandalwood) is best classified as
questions.explanation: चन्दनस्य भारं वहति इति — the final member वाही comes from the root वह् with an उपपद.

questions.explanation: The first member stands in the genitive relation (मुखस्य दोषः) — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष.

questions.question: The compound 'अल्पज्ञः' is explained as
questions.explanation: 'One who knows little' — उपपद-तत्पुरुष with the root ज्ञा.

questions.question: The verb form 'जानासि' is in which लकार?
questions.explanation: जानासि = you know — present tense, लट् लकार.

questions.question: 'जानासि' is in which person (पुरुष)?
questions.explanation: The -सि ending marks मध्यमपुरुष एकवचन: 'you know'.

questions.question: The verb form 'वद' (speak!) is in which लकार?
questions.explanation: वद is the imperative (command) form — लोट् लकार, मध्यमपुरुष एकवचन.

questions.question: The verb form 'ब्रूयात्' (one should speak) is in which लकार?
questions.explanation: ब्रूयात् expresses 'should/ought to' — विधिलिङ् लकार.

questions.question: In the verse, 'विवादाय' (for quarrel) is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: The dative of purpose: विवादाय = for the sake of quarrel.

questions.question: 'मुखदोषेण' (by the fault of the mouth) is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: The -एण ending marks तृतीया — the means/cause 'by'.

questions.question: 'पुस्तके' (in the book) is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: The -ए ending on the a-stem marks सप्तमी — place 'in/at'.

questions.question: In 'आत्मनो मुखदोषेण', the word 'आत्मनः' is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: आत्मनः = 'of their own (self)' — genitive qualifying मुखदोषेण.

questions.question: 'जानामि' (I know) is in which person (पुरुष)?
options: no person — it is a participle
questions.explanation: The -मि ending marks उत्तमपुरुष एकवचन: 'I know'.

questions.question: The form 'वदिष्यामि' (I shall speak) is in which लकार?
questions.explanation: The -इष्यामि ending marks the simple future, लृट् लकार.

questions.question: 'न जानामि' translates to
questions.explanation: न (not) + जानामि (I know) = I do not know.

questions.question: 'त्वं किं जानासि?' translates to
questions.explanation: त्वम् (you) किम् (what) जानासि (know) — the pandit's mocking question.

questions.question: 'अहं गर्वं त्यजामि' translates to
questions.explanation: अहम् (I) गर्वम् (pride) त्यजामि (abandon).

questions.question: 'कृषकः क्षेत्रं कर्षति' translates to
questions.explanation: कृषकः (farmer) क्षेत्रम् (field) कर्षति (ploughs).

questions.question: 'मौनं भज' translates to
questions.explanation: मौनम् (silence) भज (resort to/practise — लोट्).

questions.question: 'त्वम् एव मम गुरुः' translates to
questions.explanation: त्वम् (you) एव (alone/indeed) मम (my) गुरुः (guru).

questions.question: The title 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' means 'If you know, then speak.'
questions.explanation: यदि = if, जानासि = you know, तद् = then, वद = speak.

questions.question: In the dialogue, the pandit answered all of the farmer's questions about sowing, clouds and soil correctly.
questions.explanation: The pandit had to say 'न जानामि' (I do not know) to every practical question.

questions.question: At the end of the dialogue, the pandit calls the farmer his guru.
questions.explanation: अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः — today you alone are my guru.

questions.question: According to the verse 'विद्या विवादाय...', for a खल (wicked person) learning serves quarrelling.
questions.explanation: खलस्य विद्या विवादाय — the wicked person's learning is for quarrel.

questions.question: The word 'मौनम्' means speech.
questions.explanation: मौनम् means silence, not speech (which is वाक्/भाषणम्).

questions.question: The verse 'आत्मनो मुखदोषेण...' teaches that parrots and mynas are caught because of their own chattering.
questions.explanation: मुखदोषेण = by the fault of their own mouths — careless speech traps the speaker.

questions.question: According to this chapter, boasting about one's learning is a sign of true knowledge.
questions.explanation: Boasting is the mark of hollow learning; real knowledge shows in conduct and humble speech.

questions.question: The form 'तद् वद' arises from तत् + वद by sandhi.
questions.explanation: त् becomes द् before the voiced व् — जश्त्व sandhi.

questions.question: The verb form 'ब्रूयात्' (one should speak) is in लोट् लकार.
questions.explanation: ब्रूयात् is विधिलिङ् (optative, 'should'); लोट् is the imperative like वद.

questions.question: 'न जानामि' translates to 'I do not know.'
questions.explanation: न (not) + जानामि (I know).

questions.question: Complete the farmer's refrain: यदि जानासि तद् ____।
questions.explanation: यदि जानासि तद् वद — if you know, then speak.

questions.question: Complete the pandit's closing words: अद्य त्वम् एव मम ____।
questions.explanation: अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः — today you alone are my guru.

questions.question: Complete the farmer's statement about knowledge: ज्ञानं तु ____ दृश्यते।
questions.explanation: ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते — knowledge is seen in conduct.

questions.question: Complete the verse line (of the खल): विद्या ____ धनं मदाय।
questions.explanation: खलस्य विद्या विवादाय, धनं मदाय — learning for quarrel, wealth for arrogance.

questions.question: Complete the verse line: मौनं ____साधनम्।
questions.explanation: मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् — silence is the accomplisher of all aims.

questions.question: Complete the verse line: सत्यं ब्रूयात् ____ ब्रूयात्।
questions.explanation: सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात् — speak the truth, speak what is pleasant.

questions.question: The Sanskrit word for 'cloud' used in the dialogue is ____.
questions.explanation: कीदृशः मेघः वृष्टिं ददाति — what kind of cloud gives rain?

questions.question: The word 'वृष्टिः' means ____ in English.
questions.explanation: वृष्टिः = rain, from the root वृष् (to shower).

questions.question: The word 'अल्पज्ञः' means 'one who knows ____'.
questions.explanation: अल्पम् = little; अल्पं जानाति इति अल्पज्ञः.

questions.question: The Sanskrit word for 'silence', praised in the verse of the birds, is ____.
questions.explanation: मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् — silence accomplishes all aims.

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद: तद् वद = ____ + वद।
questions.explanation: तत् + वद → तद् वद (त् → द् before व्, जश्त्व).

questions.question: सन्धि: न + अस्ति = ____।
questions.explanation: अ + अ → आ (दीर्घ-सन्धि): नास्ति.

questions.question: The verb 'जानासि' (you know) is in ____ लकार।
questions.explanation: Present tense = लट् लकार.

questions.question: The verb 'वद' (speak!) is in ____ लकार।
questions.explanation: The imperative (command) = लोट् लकार.

questions.question: In the verse, 'विवादाय' (for quarrel) is in ____ विभक्ति।
questions.explanation: The dative of purpose — चतुर्थी विभक्ति.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the title 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' and why it suits this chapter.
questions.answer: The title means 'If you know, then speak.' It suits the chapter because the whole lesson turns on this rule: the pandit who boasted of knowing everything could not answer simple practical questions, while the humble farmer spoke only of what he truly knew. The title is the farmer's refrain and the chapter's central test of real knowledge.
questions.explanation: Title meaning plus its role as the refrain and moral test of the dialogue.

questions.question: What are the two central teachings (the 'twin disciplines') of this chapter?
questions.answer: (1) Real knowledge is proved in conduct (आचारे), not in loud claims or boasting — the shastra sits in the book, knowledge is seen in behaviour. (2) Speech must be disciplined: speak only of what you truly know, and honestly say 'न जानामि' about what you do not, learning it with humility and reverence.
questions.explanation: Conduct as the proof of knowledge, and certainty/honesty as the rule of speech.

questions.question: How was knowledge traditionally tested in the guru-shishya tradition, and how does the refrain 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' fit that tradition?
questions.answer: In the guru-shishya tradition the guru tested students with sharp, often riddling questions; a student's knowledge was proved by answering, and honesty was proved by admitting 'न जानामि' when the answer was unknown. The refrain 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' captures exactly this classroom rule — speak if you truly know, otherwise admit ignorance and learn.
questions.explanation: Testing through questions plus the honest refrain of admitting ignorance.

questions.question: Which three branches of learning did the pandit claim to know, and in which words?
questions.answer: The pandit claimed to know grammar, astrology and logic: व्याकरणं जानामि, ज्योतिषं जानामि, तर्कशास्त्रं च जानामि — 'I know grammar, I know astrology, and I know logic.' He then mockingly asked the farmer, त्वं किं जानासि? (What do you know?)
questions.explanation: The pandit's boast lists व्याकरण, ज्योतिष and तर्कशास्त्र.

questions.question: How does the farmer describe his own work and knowledge at the start of the dialogue?
questions.answer: The farmer humbly calls himself अल्पज्ञः (one who knows little) and describes his work in three verbs: क्षेत्रं कर्षामि (I plough the field), बीजं वपामि (I sow the seed), धान्यं च प्राप्नोमि (and I obtain grain). He then asks permission to put a question — यदि जानासि तद् वद.
questions.explanation: Self-description as अल्पज्ञ plus the three verbs of his daily work.

questions.question: Describe how the pandit changes by the end of the dialogue. Quote at least one Sanskrit sentence in your answer.
questions.answer: The pandit changes from arrogance to humility. At first he boasts, अहं सर्वाणि शास्त्राणि जानामि (I know all the shastras). After failing the farmer's practical questions, he says with humility: अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः (today you alone are my guru) and अहं गर्वं त्यजामि (I abandon my pride). He vows to speak only what he knows (यत् जानामि तत् एव वदिष्यामि) and to ask about the rest with reverence (श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि).
questions.explanation: Transformation from गर्व to विनय, with the closing vows.

questions.question: Give the अन्वय and meaning of: आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः । बकास्तत्र न बध्यन्ते मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् ॥
questions.answer: अन्वयः: शुकसारिकाः आत्मनः मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते; बकाः तत्र न बध्यन्ते; (अतः) मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्। Meaning: Parrots and mynas are caught because of the fault of their own mouths — their chattering betrays them; herons, which keep silent, are not caught; therefore silence is the accomplisher of all aims.
questions.explanation: Prose order plus translation; the verse praises disciplined silence.

questions.question: In the verse 'विद्या विवादाय...', what do विद्या, धन and शक्ति become in the hands of the खल and of the साधु respectively?
questions.answer: For the खल (wicked): विद्या serves विवाद (quarrelling), धन serves मद (arrogance), and शक्ति serves परेषां परिपीडन (tormenting others). For the साधु (noble) the same three serve the opposite ends: विद्या serves ज्ञान (wisdom), धन serves दान (charity), and शक्ति serves रक्षण (protection of others).
questions.explanation: The three possessions and their opposite uses — खल vs साधु.

questions.question: Explain the simile in 'यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य' and state what the verse says about such students of shastra.
questions.answer: The simile: a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows only the load's weight (भारस्य वेत्ता), not the sandalwood's fragrance or worth (न तु चन्दनस्य). The verse applies this to people who study many shastras but remain deluded about their meanings (अर्थेषु मूढाः) — they merely carry the texts like the donkey (खरवद्वहन्ति). Study without understanding is a burden, not knowledge.
questions.explanation: Weight vs fragrance; rote carrying of texts vs grasping their meaning.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: अल्पज्ञः, वपनम्, विचिन्त्य, योग्या, पठितवान्.
questions.answer: अल्पज्ञः = one who knows little; वपनम् = sowing; विचिन्त्य = having thought; योग्या = fit/suitable (feminine); पठितवान् = has read/studied.
questions.explanation: All five words occur in the pandit-farmer dialogue.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: परिपीडनाय, वेत्ता, अधीत्य, मूढाः, अनृतम्.
questions.answer: परिपीडनाय = for tormenting/oppressing; वेत्ता = knower; अधीत्य = having studied; मूढाः = the deluded/foolish; अनृतम् = falsehood.
questions.explanation: All five words occur in the verses of the lesson.

questions.question: Why is careless speech dangerous, according to the verse of the शुकसारिकाः? Give one modern example.
questions.answer: Careless speech betrays and traps the speaker, just as the chattering of parrots and mynas leads to their capture while the silent heron goes free. Modern example: a student who boasts or gossips carelessly (for instance posting unverified claims online) invites trouble and loses trust, while one who speaks thoughtfully and only with knowledge is respected and safe.
questions.explanation: मुखदोष = self-inflicted harm through speech; any sensible modern parallel is acceptable.

questions.question: Explain the statement 'शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते' in your own words.
questions.answer: The sentence means: the shastra (text) merely sits in the book, but knowledge is seen in conduct. Owning or memorising texts is not knowledge; knowledge exists only when learning changes how a person acts, works and behaves. The pandit had the texts; the farmer had the conduct — so the farmer possessed real knowledge of his field of life.
questions.explanation: Books store text; only conduct proves that knowledge is real.

questions.question: State three rules of disciplined speech that this chapter teaches, each supported by a phrase from the lesson.
questions.answer: (1) Speak only what you truly know — यदि जानासि तद् वद; admit the rest with 'न जानामि'. (2) Prefer purposeful silence to careless chatter — मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम्, for careless speech traps like the parrot's chattering (मुखदोषेण). (3) Let speech be both true and kind — सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात्; never a harsh truth (न ब्रूयात् सत्यमप्रियम्) nor a pleasant lie (प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयात्).
questions.explanation: Certainty, restraint and truth-with-kindness — the chapter's three rules of speech.

questions.question: "The farmer, though अल्पज्ञ by his own description, is the true विद्वान् of the story." Do you agree? Give two reasons from the text.
questions.answer: Yes. Reason 1: the farmer's knowledge is proved in conduct — he ploughs, sows and harvests successfully (क्षेत्रं कर्षामि, बीजं वपामि, धान्यं च प्राप्नोमि), while the pandit cannot answer one practical question. Reason 2: the farmer follows the dharma of the learned — honest, humble speech: he claims little (अल्पज्ञः अस्मि), speaks only of what he knows, and teaches that one should say 'न जानामि' about the unknown (यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्). By both tests of the chapter — conduct and speech — the farmer is the true विद्वान्.
questions.explanation: Evaluation using the chapter's two tests: knowledge in conduct and disciplined speech.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) यद्यपि (b) सर्वार्थसाधनम् (the first join) (c) एतदपि.
questions.answer: (a) यद्यपि = यदि + अपि (इ + अ → य्, यण्-सन्धि). (b) सर्वार्थ = सर्व + अर्थ (अ + अ → आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि), giving सर्वार्थसाधनम्. (c) एतदपि = एतत् + अपि (त् → द् before the vowel, जश्त्व).
questions.explanation: यण्, दीर्घ and जश्त्व — the three sandhi types highlighted in the lesson.

questions.question: Name the समास and give the विग्रह (expansion) of: (a) शुकसारिकाः (b) तर्कशास्त्रम्.
questions.answer: (a) शुकसारिकाः = शुकाः च सारिकाः च — द्वन्द्व-समास (two coordinate members, 'parrots and mynas'). (b) तर्कशास्त्रम् = तर्कस्य शास्त्रम् — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष ('the science of logic', first member in genitive relation).
questions.explanation: द्वन्द्व joins equals; षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष subordinates the first member in the genitive.

questions.question: State the लकार of each verb form: जानाति, पृच्छ, वदेत्, पृच्छिष्यामि.
questions.answer: जानाति (he/she knows) = लट् (present). पृच्छ (ask!) = लोट् (imperative). वदेत् (one should say) = विधिलिङ् (optative). पृच्छिष्यामि (I shall ask) = लृट् (future).
questions.explanation: The four lakaras of the lesson: लट्, लोट्, विधिलिङ्, लृट्.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति and meaning-role of each word: दानाय, श्रद्धया, खलस्य, क्षेत्रे.
questions.answer: दानाय = चतुर्थी (dative of purpose) → 'for charity'. श्रद्धया = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'with reverence'. खलस्य = षष्ठी (genitive) → 'of the wicked'. क्षेत्रे = सप्तमी (locative) → 'in the field'.
questions.explanation: Purpose (चतुर्थी), means (तृतीया), possession (षष्ठी), place (सप्तमी).

questions.question: Translate into English: (a) अहं सर्वाणि शास्त्राणि जानामि। (b) कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्?
questions.answer: (a) I know all the shastras (sciences/scriptures). (b) In which month should the sowing of seeds be done?
questions.explanation: The pandit's boast and the farmer's first practical question.

questions.question: Translate into English: यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्। एषः एव विदुषः धर्मः।
questions.answer: Whoever does not know something should say 'I do not know.' This alone is the dharma (duty/mark) of the truly learned.
questions.explanation: The farmer's central teaching on honest speech.

questions.question: Translate into simple English: सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात् न ब्रूयात् सत्यमप्रियम् । प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयात् एष धर्मः सनातनः ॥
questions.answer: One should speak the truth, and speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant (harsh) truth; and one should not speak a pleasant falsehood — this is the eternal law (सनातन धर्म) of speech.
questions.explanation: The four rules of the verse: truth, pleasantness, no harsh truth, no pleasant lie.

questions.question: "यदि जानासि तद् वद — if you know, then speak." Discuss the relevance of this teaching for a student in today's world of instant opinions and social media. Support your answer with ideas and phrases from the chapter.
questions.answer: The chapter's rule of speech — speak only when you truly know — is more relevant today than ever. On social media, opinions travel instantly and boasting is rewarded with attention, so the temptation is to speak first and learn later — exactly the pandit's error of विद्या विवादाय/मदाय, using learning for show and quarrel. The chapter offers three correctives. First, certainty: before speaking or posting, ask 'do I actually know this?' — यदि जानासि तद् वद; if not, the honest words are 'न जानामि', followed by learning with श्रद्धा. Second, restraint: careless chatter traps the speaker as the parrot's chattering traps it (आत्मनो मुखदोषेण); often मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् — thoughtful silence achieves more than hasty words. Third, kindness with truth: सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात् — even a true correction should be worded pleasantly, and a pleasant lie is still forbidden. Finally, the chapter reminds us that real credibility comes not from claims but from conduct — ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते. A student who practises these rules earns trust, avoids spreading misinformation, and keeps learning instead of merely performing knowledge.
questions.explanation: Application essay: certainty, restraint, truth-with-kindness and conduct, each tied to a phrase of the lesson.

questions.question: Narrate the story of the pandit and the farmer in your own words, quoting at least three Sanskrit sentences from the dialogue, and state its moral.
questions.answer: A pandit travelling to a village saw a farmer at work and addressed him proudly: 'अहं महान् पण्डितः अस्मि... त्वं किं जानासि?' — boasting that he knew grammar, astrology and logic. The farmer humbly called himself अल्पज्ञः and described his simple work of ploughing, sowing and harvesting; then he said, 'यदि जानासि तद् वद' and asked practical questions: 'कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्?' — in which month should seeds be sown? What kind of cloud gives rain? Which soil suits grain? To each the pandit could only reply 'न जानामि'. The farmer then delivered the lesson: 'शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते' — the shastra sits in the book, but knowledge is seen in conduct; one who does not know should honestly say 'न जानामि'. Humbled, the pandit said 'अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः', abandoned his pride (अहं गर्वं त्यजामि) and vowed to speak only what he knew and ask about the rest with reverence. Moral: real knowledge is proved in conduct and humility, not in boasting; honest admission of ignorance is the beginning of true learning.
questions.explanation: Full narration with quoted lines and the twofold moral.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय, translation and detailed explanation of: यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य । एवं हि शास्त्राणि बहून्यधीत्य चार्थेषु मूढाः खरवद्वहन्ति ॥ How does this verse connect with the dialogue of the chapter?
questions.answer: अन्वयः: यथा चन्दनभारवाही खरः भारस्य वेत्ता (भवति), न तु चन्दनस्य; एवं हि बहूनि शास्त्राणि अधीत्य (अपि) अर्थेषु मूढाः (जनाः) खरवत् वहन्ति। Translation: Just as a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows only the weight, not the sandalwood, so those who study many shastras but remain deluded about their meanings merely carry them like the donkey. Explanation: Sandalwood is precious for its fragrance, but to the donkey it is only weight on its back. Likewise, texts are precious for their meaning; a student who memorises without understanding gains only the burden of words — quantity of study without quality of comprehension. Knowledge that cannot be applied or explained is a load, not learning. Connection with the dialogue: the pandit had 'carried' grammar, astrology and logic but could not apply learning to a single question of life — he was भारस्य वेत्ता, a knower of the weight. The farmer, with little text but full understanding of his work, possessed the 'fragrance'. The verse is thus the story of the chapter compressed into a simile.
questions.explanation: अन्वय + translation + burden-vs-fragrance analysis + link to the pandit.

questions.question: "Knowledge, wealth and power are neither good nor bad in themselves — the possessor decides." Evaluate this statement in the light of the verse 'विद्या विवादाय धनं मदाय...', giving one example of each pair of uses.
questions.answer: The verse supports the statement completely. It lists three possessions — विद्या (learning), धन (wealth), शक्ति (power) — and shows that each takes its moral colour from its possessor. For the खल: learning becomes a weapon of quarrel (विवादाय) — e.g. a scholar who uses arguments only to humiliate others; wealth feeds arrogance (मदाय) — e.g. a rich man flaunting luxury over the poor; power torments others (परेषां परिपीडनाय) — e.g. a strong person bullying the weak. For the साधु the same three are reversed (विपरीतमेतत्): learning ripens into wisdom shared with students (ज्ञानाय); wealth flows into charity — feeding the hungry, funding schools (दानाय); power protects — defending the weak and upholding justice (रक्षणाय). The verse therefore teaches moral responsibility: acquiring knowledge, wealth or power is not an achievement by itself; the real examination is their use. The chapter's pandit proves the point — the same विद्या that served his गर्व at the start begins to serve ज्ञान once humility enters.
questions.explanation: Evaluation with the six uses (three खल, three साधु) and concrete examples.

questions.question: "Real knowledge shows in conduct, not in words." Analyse this statement using at least three pieces of evidence from the chapter (dialogue or verses).
questions.answer: Evidence 1 — the dialogue's climax: the farmer states the principle directly, शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते — texts sit in books, knowledge is visible only in conduct. The pandit's words claimed everything; his conduct (failure at every practical question) revealed the truth. Evidence 2 — the farmer's own case: he calls himself अल्पज्ञ, yet his conduct — ploughing, sowing, harvesting successfully and speaking with perfect honesty — displays mastery of his field; his humility itself is knowledge in action. Evidence 3 — the donkey verse: यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही — one may carry many shastras yet know only their 'weight'; without understanding shown in application, study is a burden. Supporting evidence — the parrot verse: the chattering शुकसारिकाः are trapped by speech while the silent बक survives — showy words harm, disciplined behaviour protects. Together these show the chapter's test of knowledge: not 'what can you recite?' but 'what do you do, and do you speak only what you truly know?'
questions.explanation: Analysis marshalling the dialogue, the farmer's example and two verses.

questions.question: From the lesson, explain with two examples each: (a) जश्त्व सन्धि (b) दीर्घ सन्धि, and name the समास of: शुकसारिकाः, मुखदोषेण, चन्दनभारवाही, अल्पज्ञः.
questions.answer: (a) जश्त्व (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि): a voiceless stop becomes its voiced counterpart before a voiced sound. Examples: तत् + वद → तद् वद (त् → द् before व्) — the chapter's very title; एतत् + अपि → एतदपि (त् → द् before the vowel अ). (b) दीर्घ सन्धि: a simple vowel followed by a similar vowel merges into the long vowel. Examples: न + अस्ति → नास्ति (अ + अ → आ); सर्व + अर्थ → सर्वार्थ (in सर्वार्थसाधनम्). समास identification: शुकसारिकाः = शुकाः च सारिकाः च — द्वन्द्व; मुखदोषेण = मुखस्य दोषेण — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष; चन्दनभारवाही = चन्दनस्य भारं वहति इति — उपपद-तत्पुरुष; अल्पज्ञः = अल्पं जानाति इति — उपपद-तत्पुरुष.
questions.explanation: Two sandhi rules with lesson examples plus four compound identifications.

questions.question: Explain the four लकाराः illustrated in this lesson — लट्, लोट्, विधिलिङ् and लृट् — stating what each expresses, with two verb forms from the chapter for each.
questions.answer: लट् लकार expresses the present tense — action happening now: जानामि (I know), जानासि (you know); also कर्षामि, तिष्ठति, बध्यन्ते. लोट् लकार expresses command or request (imperative): वद (speak!), पृच्छ (ask!); also भज (practise!). विधिलिङ् लकार expresses 'should/ought to' (optative/injunction): ब्रूयात् (one should speak — four times in the सत्यं ब्रूयात् verse), वदेत् (one should say — यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्). लृट् लकार expresses the future: वदिष्यामि (I shall speak), पृच्छिष्यामि (I shall ask) — the pandit's closing vows. The title itself pairs two lakaras meaningfully: जानासि (लट् — do you presently, actually know?) is the condition for वद (लोट् — the command to speak).
questions.explanation: Function of each lakara with forms drawn from the dialogue and verses.

questions.question:
Translate the closing passage of the dialogue into English and comment on its significance:
पण्डितः — भोः मित्र! अद्य त्वम् एव मम गुरुः। अहं गर्वं त्यजामि। इतः परं यत् जानामि तत् एव वदिष्यामि, यत् न जानामि तत् श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि।
questions.answer: Translation: The pandit (says) — 'O friend! Today you alone are my guru. I abandon my pride. From now on I shall speak only what I know, and what I do not know I shall ask about with reverence.' Significance: This passage is the resolution of the whole chapter. The pandit now addresses the farmer as मित्र (friend) and गुरु — the social pride that opened the dialogue ('what do YOU know?') has dissolved. His two vows restate the chapter's twin disciplines in first person: certainty in speech (यत् जानामि तत् एव वदिष्यामि — only what I know will I speak) and humility in learning (श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि — I will ask with reverence). The future-tense forms (वदिष्यामि, पृच्छिष्यामि — लृट्) show that the lesson has become a resolution for life, not merely a moment of embarrassment. True education, the passage suggests, begins the day we can say 'न जानामि' without shame.
questions.explanation: Accurate translation plus commentary on the transformation and the two vows.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions:
'पण्डितः — भोः कृषक! अहं महान् पण्डितः अस्मि। व्याकरणं जानामि, ज्योतिषं जानामि, तर्कशास्त्रं च जानामि। त्वं किं जानासि?
कृषकः — आर्य! अहम् अल्पज्ञः कृषकः अस्मि। क्षेत्रं कर्षामि, बीजं वपामि, धान्यं च प्राप्नोमि।'
(a) What three subjects does the pandit claim to know? (b) What word does the farmer use for himself, and what does it mean? (c) Which three actions make up the farmer's work? (d) What contrast of character do these two speeches reveal?
questions.answer: (a) Grammar (व्याकरणम्), astrology (ज्योतिषम्) and logic (तर्कशास्त्रम्). (b) अल्पज्ञः — 'one who knows little'. (c) He ploughs the field (क्षेत्रं कर्षामि), sows the seed (बीजं वपामि) and obtains grain (धान्यं प्राप्नोमि). (d) The pandit's speech is boastful and belittling ('what do YOU know?'), showing गर्व; the farmer's speech is modest and factual, showing विनय — pride versus humility, claims versus concrete work.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of the opening exchange and its contrast of गर्व and विनय.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions:
'कृषकः — आर्य! भवान् बहूनि शास्त्राणि पठितवान्, किन्तु जीवनस्य विद्यां न जानाति। शास्त्रं पुस्तके तिष्ठति, ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते। यः यत् न जानाति सः न जानामि इति वदेत्। एषः एव विदुषः धर्मः।'
(a) What has the pandit read, and what does he still not know? (b) Where does shastra 'sit', and where is knowledge 'seen'? (c) What should a person say about what he does not know? (d) What, according to the farmer, is the dharma of the truly learned?
questions.answer: (a) He has read many shastras (बहूनि शास्त्राणि पठितवान्) but does not know the knowledge of life (जीवनस्य विद्याम्). (b) Shastra sits in the book (पुस्तके); knowledge is seen in conduct (आचारे). (c) He should say 'न जानामि' — 'I do not know.' (d) Honest speech about one's knowledge — admitting ignorance plainly and speaking only what one knows — is the dharma of the विद्वान्.
questions.explanation: The farmer's verdict — the doctrinal core of the chapter.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer the questions:
'विद्या विवादाय धनं मदाय शक्तिः परेषां परिपीडनाय ।
खलस्य साधोर्विपरीतमेतत् ज्ञानाय दानाय च रक्षणाय ॥'
(a) Whose learning serves quarrel? (b) What does the साधु do with wealth? (c) Which word in the verse signals that the noble person's uses are 'the opposite'? (d) Which three dative (चतुर्थी) words describe the साधु's uses?
questions.answer: (a) The खल's (wicked person's) learning serves quarrel — खलस्य विद्या विवादाय. (b) The साधु uses wealth for charity — दानाय. (c) विपरीतम् ('the opposite') — साधोर्विपरीतमेतत्. (d) ज्ञानाय (for wisdom), दानाय (for charity), रक्षणाय (for protection).
questions.explanation: Close reading of the verse's structure and its datives of purpose.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer the questions:
'यथा खरश्चन्दनभारवाही भारस्य वेत्ता न तु चन्दनस्य ।
एवं हि शास्त्राणि बहून्यधीत्य चार्थेषु मूढाः खरवद्वहन्ति ॥'
(a) What does the donkey carry? (b) Of what is the donkey a 'knower', and of what is it not? (c) Who are compared to the donkey? (d) What one-word adverb in the verse means 'like a donkey'?
questions.answer: (a) A load of sandalwood (चन्दनभारः). (b) It is a knower of the weight (भारस्य वेत्ता) but not of the sandalwood — its fragrance and value (न तु चन्दनस्य). (c) Those who study many shastras yet remain deluded about their meanings (अर्थेषु मूढाः). (d) खरवत् — 'like a donkey'.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of the simile's four elements including the -वत् suffix.

questions.question:
Read the situation and answer the questions:
Rohan has read one article about a science topic and immediately lectures his whole class about it, mocking a classmate who asks careful questions. When the teacher asks Rohan a basic question on the same topic, he cannot answer.
(a) Which character of the chapter does Rohan resemble, and why? (b) Which verse-image best fits his showy talk that ends in embarrassment? (c) What should Rohan have said when the teacher asked, according to the chapter? (d) State the chapter's rule that would have saved him.
questions.answer: (a) The pandit — he boasts of knowledge he has not truly mastered and belittles others (विद्या विवादाय/मदाय). (b) The parrot of 'आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः' — his own showy speech traps him; the silent, careful classmate is like the बक. (One may also cite the donkey carrying sandalwood — text without understanding.) (c) He should have honestly said 'न जानामि' — I do not know — and asked to learn with श्रद्धा. (d) यदि जानासि तद् वद — speak only if you truly know; otherwise keep silence or admit ignorance.
questions.explanation: Application of the chapter's characters, verses and rule to a classroom scenario.

questions.question:
Read the situation and answer the questions:
Two students top the same exam. Meera quietly helps weaker classmates with their doubts and admits openly when a question is beyond her. Tanya constantly announces her rank, argues to prove others wrong, and never admits a mistake.
(a) Match each student to खल-pattern or साधु-pattern of the verse विद्या विवादाय, with the fitting Sanskrit word for each use of learning. (b) Whose knowledge would the farmer of the dialogue call real, and why? (c) Which of the chapter's twin disciplines does Meera's 'admitting openly' show?
questions.answer: (a) Tanya follows the खल pattern — her विद्या serves विवादाय (quarrelling/proving others wrong) and मदाय (pride in rank). Meera follows the साधु pattern — her विद्या serves ज्ञानाय (real understanding) and, through helping, works like दानाय (giving/sharing). (b) Meera's — because her knowledge shows in conduct (आचारे): she applies it, shares it and speaks honestly; the farmer's test is ज्ञानं तु आचारे दृश्यते. (c) The discipline of honest speech — saying 'न जानामि' about what one does not know, the mark of the विद्वान् (एषः एव विदुषः धर्मः).
questions.explanation: Evaluation applying the खल-साधु contrast and the chapter's twin disciplines.

questions.question:
Read the sentence from the dialogue and answer the grammar questions:
'इतः परं यत् जानामि तत् एव वदिष्यामि, यत् न जानामि तत् श्रद्धया पृच्छिष्यामि।'
(a) Identify the लकार of वदिष्यामि and पृच्छिष्यामि. (b) Identify the लकार and पुरुष of जानामि. (c) State the विभक्ति of श्रद्धया and its meaning-role. (d) Translate the whole sentence into English.
questions.answer: (a) Both वदिष्यामि (I shall speak) and पृच्छिष्यामि (I shall ask) are लृट् लकार (future tense). (b) जानामि is लट् लकार (present), उत्तमपुरुष (first person) एकवचन — 'I know'. (c) श्रद्धया is तृतीया (instrumental) विभक्ति — 'with reverence/faith' (manner/means). (d) 'From now on I shall speak only what I know, and what I do not know I shall ask about with reverence.'
questions.explanation: Grammar analysis of the pandit's closing vow: लृट्, लट्, तृतीया and translation.

questions.question:
Read the verse line and answer the grammar questions:
'सत्यं ब्रूयात् प्रियं ब्रूयात् न ब्रूयात् सत्यमप्रियम्।'
(a) Which लकार is ब्रूयात्, and what sense does it express? (b) What is the विभक्ति of सत्यम् and प्रियम् here, and why? (c) Split the सन्धि in सत्यमप्रियम्. (d) Give one verb from the chapter's dialogue in the same लकार as ब्रूयात्.
questions.answer: (a) ब्रूयात् is विधिलिङ् लकार — it expresses 'should/ought to' (an injunction), प्रथमपुरुष एकवचन. (b) सत्यम् and प्रियम् are in द्वितीया (accusative) विभक्ति — they are the objects of ब्रूयात् ('one should speak WHAT? — the truth, the pleasant'). (c) सत्यमप्रियम् = सत्यम् + अप्रियम्. (d) वदेत् ('one should say', in यः यत् न जानाति सः 'न जानामि' इति वदेत्) is also विधिलिङ्.
questions.explanation: विधिलिङ् recognition, accusative objects, sandhi split and a parallel form.

questions.question:
Read the exchange and answer the questions:
'कृषकः — कस्मिन् मासे बीजानां वपनं कर्तव्यम्?
पण्डितः — (विचिन्त्य) एतत्... एतत् न जानामि।
कृषकः — कीदृशः मेघः वृष्टिं ददाति? कीदृशी भूमिः धान्याय योग्या?
पण्डितः — एतदपि न जानामि।'
(a) Translate the farmer's first question. (b) Translate the farmer's last question. (c) What does विचिन्त्य tell us about the pandit's state? (d) What does the repetition of 'न जानामि' achieve in the story?
questions.answer: (a) 'In which month should the sowing of seeds be done?' (b) 'What kind of soil is fit for grain?' (c) विचिन्त्य ('having thought/pondered') shows the pandit genuinely searching his learning and finding nothing — his hesitation before admitting ignorance. (d) The repetition of 'न जानामि' hammers home the collapse of his boast 'अहं सर्वाणि शास्त्राणि जानामि'; each admission deepens his humbling and prepares his transformation, while also modelling the honest phrase the chapter recommends.
questions.explanation: Translation of the questions plus literary effect of विचिन्त्य and the repeated admission.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer the questions:
'आत्मनो मुखदोषेण बध्यन्ते शुकसारिकाः ।
बकास्तत्र न बध्यन्ते मौनं सर्वार्थसाधनम् ॥'
(a) Translate the first line. (b) Translate the second line. (c) Name the two birds that are caught and the bird that is not. (d) In one sentence, connect this verse to the farmer's advice 'यदि न जानासि तर्हि मौनं भज'.
questions.answer: (a) 'Parrots and mynas are caught (bound) by the fault of their own mouths.' (b) 'Herons are not caught there; silence is the accomplisher of all aims.' (c) Caught: the parrot (शुकः) and the myna (सारिका); not caught: the heron (बकः). (d) Both teach the same speech discipline — where knowledge (or need) to speak is absent, silence protects: the farmer tells the pandit to practise मौन exactly as the verse praises the silent heron over the chattering birds.
questions.explanation: Line-by-line translation and the link between the verse and the dialogue's advice.
